opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we looked at fairly carefully at Epoch. The basic question was: if you take the trend we've seen, training compute for frontier models growing roughly four to five times per year, can that be sustained through the end of the decade? Our tentative answer was that it looks feasible, though it gets harder over time.

The way we approached it was to look at the main bottlenecks one at a time. Probably the most important is power. Frontier training runs already need tens to hundreds of megawatts, and if you extrapolate to 2030 you're talking about multiple gigawatts for a single run. That's a lot. But there are ways around it: building dedicated generation, using natural gas or solar plus storage, and, importantly, distributing training across multiple data centers in different regions so you're not limited by what one grid connection can provide. When you account for geographically distributed training, the power constraint loosens quite a bit.

The second is chip manufacturing. Here the constraints are things like advanced packaging capacity and high-bandwidth memory production rather than the wafers themselves. TSMC and the memory makers have been expanding capacity aggressively, and our estimates suggested that enough accelerators could plausibly be produced to support runs several thousand times larger than GPT-4 by 2030, with a lot of uncertainty around that.

Third is data. People worry we're running out of high-quality text. There's something to that. The stock of public human-generated text is finite, and we may get close to using all of it within the next several years. But you have multimodal data like images, video, and audio, and increasingly synthetic data and reinforcement-learning-style approaches, where the model generates its own training signal. So data is a real constraint, but I don't think it's a hard wall in this timeframe.

The fourth is latency. As models get bigger, there's a minimum time each training step takes, which in principle limits how large a run you can finish in a reasonable period. But by our estimates that only really bites at scales beyond what's likely by 2030.

Put together, the binding constraints seem to be power and chip production, and they suggest runs around 10^29 FLOP or so could be technically feasible by the end of the decade. That's roughly ten thousand times GPT-4.

The important caveat is that technical feasibility isn't the same as it actually happening. The bigger question might be economic: will companies be willing to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on a single training run, or on the infrastructure behind it? That depends on whether the returns from AI keep justifying the investment. If models keep getting substantially more capable and generating real revenue, I think investors and companies will keep scaling. If progress disappoints, the money could dry up well before the physical constraints bind. So in some sense the physical bottlenecks give you a ceiling, and whether we hit it is a question about the economics and how valuable these systems turn out to be.

r002.rationale: It describes a projected run as roughly 10,000 times GPT-4, but does not compare this decade’s increase with the compute increase from GPT-2 to GPT-4.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we spent a lot of time on at Epoch, and I think the short answer is that it looks feasible, but it's much less obvious than people sometimes assume. The way we approached it was to decompose the problem into the main constraints that could bind, and then ask, for each of them, whether it's plausible to keep up the pace through the end of the decade.

The first constraint is power. If you extrapolate four times per year growth from where we are now, by around 2030 you're talking about training runs that require on the order of several gigawatts, maybe up to ten gigawatts for the very largest runs. That's a lot. That's comparable to the output of several large nuclear plants, or a meaningful fraction of a US state's electricity consumption. But it's not physically impossible. The US grid has a lot of capacity, there's a lot of planned capacity expansion, and you can also do things like distributed training across multiple data centers in different locations, which relaxes the constraint on any single site. So power is a real bottleneck, but it seems like a solvable one if there's enough willingness to invest.

The second is chip manufacturing. Here you have to look at TSMC's advanced node capacity and, maybe more importantly, advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory, which have been the actual bottlenecks recently. If you ask how many H100-equivalents could plausibly be produced by 2030, our estimate is that it's enough to support training runs that are many orders of magnitude larger than what we have today. So again, this doesn't seem like the thing that stops you, provided that AI continues to command a large share of the leading-edge capacity.

The third is data. For language models, if you keep scaling at the current rate, you run out of high-quality public text data sometime around the end of the decade. But there are a number of ways around this. You can train for multiple epochs with fairly modest penalties, you can use multimodal data, and there's synthetic data, which is still somewhat uncertain but looks promising. So I'd say data is a constraint that slows things down somewhat rather than a hard wall.

And the fourth is what we call the latency wall, which is basically that as you scale the number of chips, the time it takes to do a single forward and backward pass over the network imposes a floor, and that limits how many sequential steps you can do within a given training run. That one is more of a long-run limit, and I don't think it binds before 2030, although it depends on batch size scaling and some other things.

So when you put all of this together, our conclusion is that something like four times per year through 2030 is feasible on the supply side, with power probably being the tightest. The bigger uncertainty, honestly, is on the demand side. These runs would cost on the order of hundreds of billions of dollars, maybe approaching a trillion in total capex across the ecosystem. Whether that money actually gets spent depends on whether the labs and their investors keep seeing returns, whether AI revenue grows fast enough to justify it. And that's a question about economics and about how useful the models turn out to be, not about physics or manufacturing. My own view is that the willingness is probably there, because the payoff from being first to very capable systems is enormous, but I'd put more of the probability mass on an economic slowdown than on a hard technical bottleneck.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s feasible, but it’s far from guaranteed. Four times per year is a very rapid rate of growth: over five years, that’s roughly a thousandfold increase in the compute used for a training run. So the question is whether the resources needed to support that can grow sufficiently quickly.

I’d distinguish a few constraints. One is power: can you build the data centers and secure the electricity connections? Another is chip supply, including advanced packaging and memory. A third is whether you can get an increasingly large number of chips to work together efficiently. And then there’s the economic question: are companies willing to spend the money?

You don’t need spending or electricity consumption to rise by four times every year, because hardware efficiency improves. But those improvements only get you part of the way. You still need substantial increases in investment and infrastructure, and those take time to deliver.

My assessment would be that continuing at something like that rate through 2030 is a plausible scenario. I wouldn’t treat it as an inevitable extrapolation. In particular, the willingness to invest depends on whether scaling continues to produce capabilities that generate enough economic value. Something can be technically achievable and still turn out not to be economically attractive.

r001.rationale: The response calls this growth a plausible scenario but says it is far from guaranteed and not inevitable; it does not judge it likely.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s feasible, but it’s far from guaranteed. Four times per year means roughly a thousandfold increase over five years, so this is a substantial expansion. You have to ask whether chip production, power, the ability to connect large numbers of chips together, and the financing can all keep up.

Power is one of the more difficult constraints because the infrastructure takes time to build. It’s not enough to purchase the chips; you need a site that can supply electricity and cooling, and you need the networking to use those chips effectively in a single training run.

The economic side is also important. Companies have to be willing to spend increasingly large sums, and that depends on whether they continue to see valuable improvements from scaling. So I’d distinguish between what’s physically possible and what will actually happen. I don’t see a decisive reason that this rate must stop before 2030, but sustaining it requires several things to go right simultaneously.
